t: The three basic financial decisions a finance manager takes are usually classified as:
e: Financial management is built around the investment (capital budgeting) decision, the financing (capital structure) decision and the dividend decision; the other options are operational or accounting activities.

t: An insurer's finance head wants to decide whether to raise ₹200 crore through subordinated debt or fresh equity. This is primarily a/an:
e: Choosing the mix of debt and equity to fund the company is the financing (capital structure) decision; how the funds are then deployed would be the investment decision.

t: A cost that remains unchanged in total within the relevant range irrespective of the number of policies issued is a:
e: Fixed costs such as office rent and depreciation do not change in total with activity within the relevant range, although fixed cost per unit falls as volume rises.

t: Policy stamp duty paid per policy and commission paid at a fixed percentage of premium are examples of:
o: Period costs that are also fixed
e: Both costs vary in direct proportion to the number of policies or premium volume, which is the defining feature of a variable cost.

t: An insurer spent ₹3 crore last year on a core-system that is now obsolete. In deciding whether to buy a new system, this ₹3 crore is a:
e: A sunk cost has already been incurred and cannot be recovered by any future decision, so it is irrelevant to the replacement decision.

t: A branch's telephone bill is ₹8,000 per month when 2,000 calls are made and ₹11,000 when 5,000 calls are made. Using the high-low method, the fixed element of the cost per month is:
A firm has EBIT of ₹30 lakh and annual interest of ₹6 lakh. Its interest coverage ratio is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ Interest = 30 ÷ 6 = 5 times, indicating comfortable ability to service debt.

t: Under marginal costing, which of the following is treated as a period cost and charged fully to the profit and loss account of the period?
e: Marginal costing charges only variable costs to products; fixed costs are treated as period costs written off in full against contribution for the period.

t: Contribution is defined as:
e: Contribution = Sales − Variable cost; it 'contributes' first to recovering fixed cost and then to profit, so it also equals Fixed cost + Profit.

t: A health insurer sells a policy at ₹5,000 premium with variable cost (commission, stamp, medical tests) of ₹2,000 per policy. Fixed costs of the product line are ₹60 lakh per year. The break-even number of policies is:
e: Contribution per policy = 5,000 − 2,000 = ₹3,000. Break-even units = Fixed cost ÷ Contribution per unit = 60,00,000 ÷ 3,000 = 2,000 policies.

t: A company has sales of ₹40 lakh, variable cost of ₹24 lakh and fixed cost of ₹10 lakh. Its P/V ratio is:
e: P/V ratio = Contribution ÷ Sales × 100 = (40 − 24) ÷ 40 × 100 = 40%. It shows the contribution earned per rupee of sales.

t: If budgeted sales are ₹80 lakh and break-even sales are ₹60 lakh, the margin of safety ratio is:
e: Margin of safety = (Actual sales − BEP sales) ÷ Actual sales = (80 − 60) ÷ 80 = 25%. Sales can fall by 25% before a loss is incurred.

t: An increase in the selling price per unit, other factors remaining constant, will cause the break-even point to:
e: A higher selling price raises contribution per unit, so fewer units are needed to recover the same fixed cost and the break-even point falls.

t: A budget is best described as:
o: A record of past income and expenditure
A statement of assets and liabilities
A quantitative plan of action for a defined future period
A list of standard costs per unit
e: A budget is a financial and/or quantitative statement prepared in advance of a period, expressing the policy to be pursued to attain an objective.

t: In a budgeting system, the budget that is normally prepared first and on which all other functional budgets depend is the:
e: Sales is usually the principal budget factor; the premium income budget drives the expense, commission, claims and cash budgets, which are then summarised in the master budget.

t: An insurer's regional office budgets opening cash of ₹12 lakh, premium collections of ₹90 lakh, claim payments of ₹55 lakh, commission of ₹9 lakh and management expenses of ₹20 lakh for the quarter. The budgeted closing cash balance is:
e: Closing cash = 12 + 90 − 55 − 9 − 20 = ₹18 lakh. The cash budget shows receipts and payments only, not accruals.

t: Standard material cost per unit is 5 kg at ₹20 per kg. Actual usage for 1,000 units was 5,400 kg at ₹19 per kg. The material usage variance is:
e: Usage variance = (Standard quantity − Actual quantity) × Standard price = (5,000 − 5,400) × 20 = ₹8,000 Adverse, since more material was used than standard.

t: Using the data: standard 5 kg at ₹20 per kg per unit, actual 5,400 kg at ₹19 per kg for 1,000 units, the material price variance is:
e: Price variance = (Standard price − Actual price) × Actual quantity = (20 − 19) × 5,400 = ₹5,400 Favourable because the actual price was lower.

t: A division has sales of ₹200 crore, operating profit of ₹20 crore and capital employed of ₹80 crore. Its ROI is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). ROI = Operating profit ÷ Capital employed = 20 ÷ 80 = 25%. Alternatively margin 10% × turnover 2.5 = 25%.

t: Which of the following is most likely to produce a favourable labour rate variance together with an adverse labour efficiency variance?
o: Employing lower-grade, cheaper staff who take longer
Paying overtime premium to skilled staff
A rise in wage rates under a new union agreement
e: Cheaper labour reduces the rate paid (favourable rate variance) but, being less skilled, takes more hours than standard (adverse efficiency variance).

t: The principle under which only significant variances are reported to senior management for action is called:
e: Management by exception concentrates managerial attention on deviations that exceed a tolerance limit, leaving routine results to operate without intervention.

t: The current ratio of a company is computed as:
e: Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities; a ratio of 2:1 is conventionally regarded as satisfactory for manufacturing firms.

t: A company has current assets of ₹60 lakh including inventory of ₹18 lakh and prepaid expenses of ₹2 lakh, and current liabilities of ₹40 lakh. Its quick (acid-test) ratio is:
e: Quick assets = 60 − 18 − 2 = ₹40 lakh. Quick ratio = 40 ÷ 40 = 1:1. Inventory and prepaid expenses are excluded because they cannot be quickly converted to cash.

t: A company earned a net profit after tax of ₹24 crore. It has 8 crore equity shares of ₹10 each and the market price per share is ₹90. Its price-earnings ratio is:
e: EPS = 24 ÷ 8 = ₹3 per share. P/E = Market price ÷ EPS = 90 ÷ 3 = 30 times.

t: Debt-equity ratio is primarily a measure of:
e: Debt-equity ratio (long-term debt ÷ shareholders' funds) indicates the extent to which the firm relies on borrowed funds and hence its long-term solvency risk.

t: For a general insurer, the combined ratio is calculated as:
o: Claims ratio plus expense (including commission) ratio
Net premium divided by net worth
Investment income divided by net premium
e: Combined ratio = Incurred claims ratio + Expense ratio (management expenses and commission as a percentage of premium). A combined ratio above 100% means an underwriting loss.

topic: Insurance Company Accounts and Financial Reporting
t: Gross direct premium ₹800 crore, reinsurance accepted ₹50 crore, reinsurance ceded ₹250 crore. Net written premium is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Net written premium = Gross direct + Reinsurance accepted − Reinsurance ceded = 800 + 50 − 250 = ₹600 crore.

topic: Fund Flow and Cash Flow Statements
t: In a fund flow statement, 'funds' usually means:
e: Fund flow analysis traces changes in net working capital (current assets minus current liabilities) between two balance sheet dates.

topic: Fund Flow and Cash Flow Statements
t: Which of the following transactions results in a flow of funds (change in working capital)?
o: Transfer of profit to general reserve
Conversion of debentures into equity shares
e: Buying a fixed asset for cash reduces a current asset without affecting a current liability, so working capital changes. The other items affect only non-current items on both sides.

topic: Fund Flow and Cash Flow Statements
t: Under Ind AS 7 / AS 3, interest paid on borrowings by a non-financial company is classified as a cash flow from:
e: For a non-financial enterprise interest paid is treated as a cost of obtaining finance and is shown under financing activities; for a financial enterprise it is an operating cash flow.

topic: Fund Flow and Cash Flow Statements
t: Net profit for the year is ₹50 lakh after charging depreciation of ₹8 lakh and a loss on sale of asset of ₹2 lakh. Debtors increased by ₹5 lakh and creditors increased by ₹3 lakh. Cash flow from operating activities is:
e: Operating cash flow = 50 + 8 (depreciation) + 2 (loss on sale) − 5 (debtors increase) + 3 (creditors increase) = ₹58 lakh.

t: The payback period of a project is the time required for:
o: Profits to equal the initial investment
Cumulative cash inflows to equal the initial cash outflow
Depreciation to be fully written off
e: Payback measures how quickly the original investment is recovered from cash inflows; it ignores the time value of money and cash flows after payback.

t: A project costs ₹10 lakh and yields annual cash inflows of ₹2.5 lakh for 6 years. Its payback period is:
e: Payback = Initial investment ÷ Annual cash inflow = 10,00,000 ÷ 2,50,000 = 4 years.

t: A project requires an outlay of ₹5,00,000 and gives a single cash inflow of ₹6,05,000 at the end of year 2. At a 10% discount rate (PV factor 0.826), its NPV is approximately:
e: PV of inflow = 6,05,000 × 0.826 ≈ ₹5,00,000, so NPV ≈ 0; the project earns exactly the 10% cost of capital.

t: The internal rate of return (IRR) of a project is the discount rate at which:
o: Accounting rate of return equals cost of capital
e: IRR is the rate that equates the present value of cash inflows with the initial outlay, making NPV zero; a project is accepted if IRR exceeds the cost of capital.

t: The qualifying examination for an individual insurance agent conducted by the Insurance Institute of India is:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). IC-38 is the agents' pre-recruitment examination; IC-01/02/11/14 are Licentiate papers.

t: Two mutually exclusive projects have NPVs of ₹12 lakh and ₹9 lakh and IRRs of 14% and 18% respectively. The cost of capital is 10%. Under the NPV rule the firm should:
o: Accept the project with ₹12 lakh NPV
e: For mutually exclusive projects NPV is the superior criterion because it measures absolute wealth added at the cost of capital; the ₹12 lakh NPV project is chosen despite its lower IRR.

t: A responsibility centre whose manager is accountable for costs, revenues and the investment base is called a/an:
e: An investment centre manager controls assets as well as profit, so performance is judged by ROI or residual income; a profit centre controls only costs and revenues.

t: A division has operating profit of ₹18 crore on an investment base of ₹120 crore. The company's required rate of return is 12%. The division's residual income is:
e: Residual income = Profit − (Investment × Required return) = 18 − (120 × 12%) = 18 − 14.4 = ₹3.6 crore.

t: The principle that a manager should be held accountable only for those costs over which he has significant influence is called the:
e: Responsibility accounting rests on controllability: reports to a manager should separate controllable from uncontrollable costs so that evaluation is fair.

t: A claims-processing department whose head is evaluated only on cost per claim settled and total departmental expense is operating as a:
e: The manager controls inputs (costs) but not revenue or investment, which makes the department a cost centre.

topic: Working Capital and Sources of Finance
t: Gross working capital refers to:
e: Gross working capital is the firm's total investment in current assets; net working capital is current assets less current liabilities.

topic: Working Capital and Sources of Finance
t: A firm has an inventory holding period of 40 days, a receivables collection period of 35 days and a payables payment period of 30 days. Its operating (cash conversion) cycle is:
e: Cash conversion cycle = Inventory days + Receivable days − Payable days = 40 + 35 − 30 = 45 days.

t: A corporate agent may tie up with a maximum of how many insurers in each line of business?
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Raised from 3 to 9 insurers per category (life, general, health) by the 2022 amendment to the Corporate Agents Regulations.

topic: Insurance Company Accounts and Financial Reporting
t: Under the IRDAI accounting regulations, the revenue account of a general insurer is prepared in:
e: Schedule B of the regulations prescribes Form B-RA (revenue account), Form B-PL (profit and loss account) and Form B-BS (balance sheet) for general insurers; the 'A' forms apply to life insurers.

topic: Insurance Company Accounts and Financial Reporting
t: A general insurer had net earned premium of ₹500 crore, net incurred claims of ₹360 crore, commission of ₹40 crore and management expenses of ₹110 crore. Its combined ratio is:
e: Claims ratio = 360 ÷ 500 = 72%; expense ratio (commission + management expenses) = 150 ÷ 500 = 30%. Combined ratio = 72% + 30% = 102%, indicating an underwriting loss.

topic: Insurance Company Accounts and Financial Reporting
t: The reserve for unexpired risk in a general insurer's accounts represents:
o: Premium received for the portion of the policy period falling after the balance sheet date
Claims intimated but not yet paid
e: Unexpired risk reserve (unearned premium) defers the part of written premium relating to risk coverage after the year-end, so that premium is recognised over the policy term.

topic: Insurance Company Accounts and Financial Reporting
t: IBNR in insurance accounting stands for a provision for claims that are:
e: IBNR covers losses that have occurred before the balance sheet date but have not yet been reported to the insurer; it is estimated actuarially and included in outstanding claims.

topic: Activity Based Costing and Pricing Decisions
t: Under activity-based costing, overheads are assigned to products using:
o: A single plant-wide rate based on direct labour hours
Cost drivers that reflect the activities consumed by each product
e: ABC traces overhead to activities (cost pools) and then to products using cost drivers such as number of policies issued or claims handled, giving more accurate product costs.

topic: Activity Based Costing and Pricing Decisions
t: An insurer's policy-issuance activity pool costs ₹60 lakh per year and 1,20,000 policies are issued. Product X uses 30,000 of these policies. The overhead charged to Product X under ABC is:
e: Cost driver rate = 60,00,000 ÷ 1,20,000 = ₹50 per policy. Overhead to Product X = 30,000 × 50 = ₹15 lakh.
